newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. sanctions panel works to speed food to Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.N. sanctions panel works to speed food to Iraq.

text.p: The United Nations sanctions committee on Iraq on Friday discussed possible changes it may implement to accelerate delivery of food to Iraqis under the ongoing oil-for-food accord.
Western diplomats on the committee said no final decisions were made on the subject. Members agreed to meet next week to possibly approve the technical changes presented.
"Nothing will change the procedures. We're looking at speeding-up the processes under the procedures," the diplomat said.

Even though Iraq has been allowed to sell limited quantities of crude oil since the start of the deal on December 10, the process of turning oil receipts into food and aid purchases has been sluggish.
"We all thought by now, near the end of the first 90-day period, that the food would have been arriving," a diplomat said.
Committee members discussed altering the way it reviews contracts for food deliveries to try to change that situation.
Currently, applications submitted for food and aid contracts are not circulated to the committee until the oil money is available in a special escrow account.
"Now, we may decide to look at the contracts a bit in advance so that any query on the contracts can be sorted out before they're actually put up for formal approval," the diplomat said.
"This means if there are any holds put on the applications for technical questions they can be sorted in advance."
Iraq has signed 31 contracts with foreign oil companies since the accord's start.

Under the deal, Baghdad is permitted to sell $2 billion worth of crude over the six-month life of the deal as a special humanitarian relief from sanctions imposed after Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990.
The deal is divided into two 90-day tranches, with each tranche to result in $1 billion worth of crude sales. The first segment of the six-month deal ends on March 9.
